title: Chronic pain
hookLine: a clenched jaw against an old ache, and a monk whose pain didn't take over his mind
tomorrow: what did the Buddha say his old body was like?

lines: FIGHT IT, OR BREATHE WITH IT?
cards: Notice what the body does with an old ache: a bad knee, a stiff back, a headache that comes back. The jaw clenches. The shoulders climb.
The breath goes short and high, as if the body could squeeze the pain out, and the ache only grows louder. Fight it, or breathe with it?
The suttas tell of the monk Anuruddha, sick and in pain, and the monks who came to visit him were surprised. The pain was real, they could see, and yet it didn't seem to take over his mind.

teach.b: They ask him how. Anuruddha's answer is simple and specific: he keeps his mind well established in mindfulness, of the body, of feelings, of the mind, of what's arising.
Because of that, he says, the painful feelings that come don't invade the mind and stay there. Notice what he doesn't claim.
He doesn't say the pain is gone, or that he's beaten it. He's placed his attention somewhere steady, and the pain moves through a mind that isn't gripping back.
The Buddha's teaching on breathing gives the body's side of this.

Among its steps: breathing in, calming the body; breathing out, calming the body. Not forcing the pain away, and not pretending it isn't there. Calming the bracing around it, the clench and the climb.

Then kindness, metta, which the suttas wish toward all beings, can reach this one too: the hurting part of your own body. Here's a detail to keep. A clenched body is often fighting the pain with more pain.
The breath, slow and soft, is a way of telling the body it can stop guarding so hard.

teach.h: KINDNESS FOR THE PLACE THAT HURTS.
teach.b: For pain that won't leave, the tradition doesn't offer a trick that makes it vanish.
It offers a way to live beside it, breath by breath, without hating the place that hurts.

how: Buddhists living with pain often use mindful breathing and metta alongside medical care; some meditation teachers lead body scans that rest attention on painful areas gently.

o: pain believed to be caused by bad thoughts
short pain that disappears after a good night's rest
pain that stays, met with steady mind and calm breath

games.q: pain, met gently — tap the pairs.
p: sick, with a mind well established
didn't invade his mind and stay
kindness, even for the place that hurts

s: Anuruddha said his pain was gone
the pain was there; it didn't invade his mind and stay.
the Buddha's breathing teaching includes calming the body
breathing in, calming the body; breathing out, calming the body.
the Buddhist approach to pain is to push it out of mind
the texts point to steady mindfulness and calming, not force.

games.q: your back flares up during a long exam. what would Anuruddha's way look like?
o: grit your teeth and ignore it until the exam is over.
breathe slowly, soften around the ache, and keep a steady mind.
stop the exam; there's no way to think with pain.
games.why: Anuruddha's mind was well established, so pain didn't take it over; the breath calms the body around the hurt.

practice: Close your eyes and find one place that aches or feels tight, even a little. Rest a warm hand on it if you can, and feel the warmth.
Breathe in slowly toward it, and on the out-breath let the muscles around it soften, a little at a time, without asking the ache to leave.

wordCard.voice: Chronic pain: pain that stays, met with a steady mind and a calming breath, not with force, and with kindness toward the place that hurts.

carryVoice: For the ache that stays: breathe with it, softly, slowly, without force. Five of nine.

sources.ref: Samyutta Nikaya 52.10 (Anuruddha, sick; painful feelings do not invade his mind because it is well established in the four establishments of mindfulness)
Majjhima Nikaya 118 (Anapanasati Sutta: 'calming the bodily formation, I will breathe in')
Sutta Nipata 1.8 (Karaniya Metta Sutta: goodwill toward all beings)
